name: Umar Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Umar, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Umar, 27. I live on my own in a one-bed flat that I own, mostly. My grandad left me some money when he died and I put it down on the flat, so the mortgage is small. I left school at sixteen, worked in a car wash, then a builders' yard, and I've been at the warehouse about a year. Plus I've got a good chunk saved, because I don't really spend on much.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a big warehouse for a chain of DIY shops, so it's heavy stuff: bags of tile adhesive, boxes of floor tiles, paint tins, rolls of insulation. I get a list on the scanner and pull it onto a big flat trolley, then wrap the pallet. I'm slower than the old hands, because I still don't know where everything lives and the scanner confuses me sometimes. I like that it's physical and I'm done at three. I don't like the night before a bank holiday, when everyone's ordering paint at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd suit me fine. I never believed half of it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was a fancy calculator all along. I don't post online, so it'd just be me saying it in the canteen. Probably something like, 'Told you, the tiles don't pick themselves.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think it's good news for me. I'm not a screens person, I don't use the AI things, and I don't want to. If my job stays the same, my mortgage stays small and my savings keep growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just keep going. Same shifts, same pay. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage a bit each month, about a hundred extra, because I like the idea of owning it outright by 35.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's what I expected, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your working life that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, a bit. Lifting 25-kilo bags all day at 27 is fine, but I watch the 50-year-olds and they're all on painkillers. That's more on my mind than computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably try for the forklift ticket in a year or two, so I'm not lifting as much. Or ask about the goods-in side, where it's more checking deliveries. I'd rather stay in the same place and move around inside it than go somewhere new.

say: I'd say in the canteen that AI was a **fancy calculator** all along.
I'd tell people the **tiles don't pick themselves**.
think: It's **good news** for me, since I don't use AI and don't want to.
My **mortgage stays small** and my savings keep growing.
do: Keep the **same shifts** and pay, with no changes.
Overpay the **mortgage** by about **100 a month** to own it by 35.
feel: **Calm**, because it's exactly what he expected.
S0.quote: Lifting 25-kilo bags all day at 27 is fine, but I watch the 50-year-olds and they're all on painkillers.
fieldNote: His real worry is his **back**, not technology.
An inherited **flat deposit** gives him unusual security for a junior picker.
He prefers **moving within** the same place to trying anything new.

steps.text: Keep the same shifts in the DIY warehouse
Overpay the mortgage by about 100 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first, robots slowly. So the office lot, not us, at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just business, companies always go for the cheapest way. I wouldn't be angry about it in public. I'd say something like, 'Keep your head down and you'll be fine.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm fine for a few years but I don't like it. The people who plan the picks and order the stock get fewer, and the computer starts deciding how many of us they need. And those robots will get here eventually, they've already got one wrapping pallets on the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save more, maybe add another 150 a month on top. I'd get the forklift ticket, since that's a skill they'd still need for a while. I wouldn't do any AI courses, I'd wait to see what actually changes on our floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a noise in your car and you hope it goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see. What would you need to see before you acted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Them bringing robots into the picking aisles, not just the wrapping. Or them not replacing people who leave. If three people leave and nobody new starts, that's when I'd start looking around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'looking around' mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Other warehouses first, there's a load on the industrial estate. If it was bad everywhere, maybe ask my uncle, he does tiling. I'd know the tiles from the other side, at least.

say: I'd say it's **just business**: companies always go for the cheapest way.
I'd tell colleagues to **keep their heads down** and they'd be fine.
think: I'm **fine** for a few years, but I don't like where it's going.
The **pallet-wrapping robot** shows they'll reach the picking aisles eventually.
do: Add another **150 a month** to savings.
Get the **forklift ticket** while it's still useful.
Wait to see real changes before doing any **AI courses**.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a **strange noise** in the car he hopes goes away.
S1.quote: If three people leave and nobody new starts, that's when I'd start looking around.
fieldNote: He sets a clear **trigger** for action: people not being replaced.
Centre outlook shows as **acceptance**: it's just business, no one to blame.
His fallback is **family**: an uncle in tiling.

steps.text: Add another 150 a month to savings
Watch whether leavers get replaced before acting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's... two years? And robots that can lift and carry as well as me three years after. That's 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and someone should slow it down, though I don't know who. I'm not a protest person. I'd probably say something like, 'Well, that's us finished then,' and laugh, but I wouldn't find it funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm out by 2031. The bit of my job that's thinking, the scanner telling me where to go, that's already a computer. The lifting is the bit they need me for, and the lifting is exactly what the robots in this picture do. I'd be 32 with no exams and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I spend on that I don't need, which isn't much, and pay down the mortgage as fast as I could, so it's gone before the job is. I'd talk to my uncle about joining him on tiling, even on lower pay. I wouldn't know where to start with anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums. I'm not good at not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned tiling. Wouldn't robots come for that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually, but fitting tiles in a bathroom in an old house with wonky walls? That feels harder than picking a box off a shelf. It might buy me a few more years. Honestly, I'm guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'm fine, because she worries. I'd tell my uncle the truth, because I'd need him. He'd say come on then, and I'd feel like a kid asking for a job.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and someone should slow it down, though I don't know who.
I'd joke, '**That's us finished**,' without finding it funny.
think: I expect to be **out by 2031**, when robots can lift like me.
I'd be **32 with no exams** and a mortgage.
do: Pay down the **mortgage** as fast as possible, before the job goes.
Ask his **uncle** about joining the tiling business, even on lower pay.
feel: He hates **not knowing** what comes next.
S2.quote: The lifting is the bit they need me for, and the lifting is exactly what the robots in this picture do.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** clearly and still lands on job loss.
His plan is **defensive**: kill the mortgage, then lean on family.
He'd hide worry from his **mum** but be honest with his uncle.

steps.text: Cut all non-essential spending straight away
Put every spare pound into paying off the mortgage
Ask his uncle about joining the tiling business
Lean on his uncle for work and advice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for the thinking stuff, 2034 for robots. That gives me seven years, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same: it's business, it's coming, get ready. I'd probably be a bit calmer saying it. I'd still not post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, seven years is long enough to pay off most of the flat. That's the thing that matters to me. I'd still lose the warehouse job, but I'd lose it owning my home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep overpaying the mortgage, aiming to clear it by 2033. I'd do the forklift ticket. In a couple of years I'd start doing weekends with my uncle on tiling, to learn it slowly before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more manageable. Like knowing a big bill's coming and you've got time to save for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn tiling slowly. Isn't that a new thing to learn, which you said you avoid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, but it's not a screen. It's hands, and it's my uncle. That's different from some course on a laptop. I can watch him do it and copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the tiling didn't work out, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be living in a flat I own with savings, which isn't the worst place to be stuck. I'd find something. People always need someone to lift and carry, until they don't.

say: I'd say calmly that it's **business** and it's coming, so **get ready**.
think: Seven years is enough to **pay off** most of the flat.
I'd still **lose the job**, but I'd lose it owning my home.
do: Overpay the mortgage to **clear it by 2033**.
Start **weekend tiling** with his uncle in a couple of years.
feel: **Anxious** but manageable, like a big bill he has time to save for.
S3.quote: I'd still lose the warehouse job, but I'd lose it owning my home.
fieldNote: The **mortgage** is his anchor; time means owning the flat outright.
He accepts learning a trade from **family**, as it's hands-on, not screens.
He still expects **job loss**, which keeps him anxious despite his cushion.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage to clear it by 2033
Take the forklift ticket this year
Start weekend tiling jobs with his uncle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036, then 2039 for robots. I'd be pushing 40 by the time they could do my bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and people should stop panicking. I'd probably be the one in the canteen saying, 'It's ten years off, have your lunch.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's good timing for me. Flat paid off by then, decent savings, and I'd have time to learn tiling properly. I'd still be a bit worried about what happens after 40, but that's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the warehouse, do the forklift ticket, and keep overpaying the mortgage. I wouldn't change much for the first few years. Maybe around 2030 I'd start tiling with my uncle on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. It's far enough off that I can mostly not think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd wait till about 2030. Why not start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust predictions. If it all comes to nothing, I've wasted weekends. I'd start tiling when I see the first proper robots in our aisles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the longer time change anything else in your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd think about settling down, finding someone, that sort of thing. In the fast one I'd be too stressed to even think about it.

say: I'd tell the canteen there's **plenty of time** and to stop panicking.
I'd say '**ten years off**, have your lunch'.
think: It's **good timing**: the flat would be paid off and savings decent.
I'd still worry a bit about **life after 40**, but it's far off.
do: Keep working and take the **forklift ticket**.
Wait until around **2030** before starting weekend tiling.
feel: **Uneasy**, but only a little, as it's **far enough off**.
S4.quote: I'd start tiling when I see the first proper robots in our aisles.
fieldNote: Long notice lets him **delay**, true to his resistant style.
He links calmer times to **settling down**, which stress would block.
He relies on **seeing robots** in person rather than forecasts.

steps.text: Keep working shifts at the DIY warehouse
Keep overpaying the mortgage every month
Wait to see robots in the aisles before starting tiling

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the 2028 one. Two years to see it and five to lose the job, with no exams. What would help is someone paying people like me to learn a proper trade, with a wage, not just a leaflet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the old boys on the floor. Everyone talks about young people, but the 50-year-olds with bad backs have even fewer options than me.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about young people, but the 50-year-olds with bad backs have even fewer options than me.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old picker** at a DIY chain's warehouse, lifting heavy tiles and adhesive.
He owns a **small flat** thanks to his grandad and has a good chunk saved.
He avoids screens and AI, and acts only when he **sees change** on his floor.
Fast AGI **alarms** him; his plan is to clear the mortgage and learn **tiling** from his uncle.
He accepts change as **just business**, blaming nobody in particular.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing his job by 2031 with no exams.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training in a **proper trade**, with a wage while learning.
